clue.text: Living things turning brown, certainly missing sun (6)

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: it names living things collectively, as one mass noun covering the whole living world.

explanation.walkthrough: Sun for S is one of the shortenings a solver simply has to own; the comma after 'brown' is the setter's punctuation and carries no instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Living things -> NATURE: the word covers the living world taken as a whole — plants, animals, everything growing — rather than any one creature.

indicators.note: something that turns ends up facing the way it came from, so the three letters for brown are written back to front
what is missing has gone from the word, so the letter named beside it never gets written

blocks.note: brown as a colour is TAN, and it arrives the other way round
certainly and surely agree, so SURE is the word to work on
the diary shortens Sunday to S, and that is the letter that walks out

clue.text: Organisation receiving articles about stomach in the ape (5-5)

explanation.walkthrough: Phi spells the ape with a final G, the older variant you will find in Chambers; 'articles' being plural is the quiet signal that the same little word appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: ape -> ORANG-UTANG: the big red tree-dwelling primate of Borneo and Sumatra, so the general word is defined by one of its species.

indicators.note: an organisation that receives something takes it indoors, so its own letters open and close round everything else
one thing placed about another sits round it, which is where the pair of little words go relative to the stomach

blocks.note: the everyday three-letter shortening of the word, split to make room
the indefinite article twice over, which is why the clue says articles rather than article
gut is the plain word for the stomach, and it goes between that pair

clue.text: According to Fleming it’s M for misbehaviour? (8)

explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a flat statement about who M is in the Bond books and it writes itself out; the question mark covers the joke of 'M for misbehaviour'.
explanation.definitionFit: misbehaviour -> MISCHIEF: playful bad behaviour of the sort children get up to, so the definition is a shade more formal than the answer.

the contraction unpacked to 'it is', and only the verb is wanted
in Ian Fleming's novels M runs the Secret Service, so his job title is the word the wordplay wants

clue.text: Legal establishments showing limits to imagination nonetheless (4)

explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal establishments' reads at first like licensed premises, which is exactly the pull the setter wants: the Inns of Court are chambers, not bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal establishments -> INNS: the four Inns of Court in London are the bodies every English barrister must belong to, so these inns are not pubs.

indicators.note: the limits of a word are where it starts and where it stops, so each word named after this gives up only its two end letters

the same treatment applied to the word that follows

clue.text: Important naval figure seen in hold? (6)

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses meet only in the spelling, and the question mark is the setter admitting how far apart they are. Capital letter or not is the solver's clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Important naval figure -> Horatio, the admiral of Trafalgar; hold -> the wrestling grip locked round an opponent from behind, two senses sharing one spelling.

clue.text: Nervous European Democrat generally cleared out (4)

explanation.walkthrough: Two of crosswording's commonest one-letter abbreviations sit side by side here; the political surface is decoration, since neither letter depends on which party.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervous -> EDGY: on edge and quick to snap, so the answer carries an irritable streak that plain nervousness does not.

the first and last letters of the word, with everything between them gone

explanation.walkthrough: Setters use Holland loosely for the whole of the Netherlands — strictly it is only two of its provinces — because the country's two-letter code is what the wordplay needs.

clue.text: Attitude after line in retreat (4)

explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' reads as one phrase about a beaten army, and that is the trap: 'in' only joins the halves, and 'retreat' on its own is the definition.

clue.text: Mum certainly tense - most likely to withdraw (6)
